vignette:
Jamil is a 55-year-old farmer who lives with his wife on the land his family has worked for three generations. He came to therapy reluctantly, at his wife's insistence, after months of what she described as him "not being himself." On the intake, he scored 76 on the PCL-5, and as he began to speak, the story of what happened to him six months ago emerged in fragments-disconnected pieces that he struggled to hold together, each one feeling as though it belonged to someone else's life.

It happened on a late afternoon in early November, just after the harvest. Jamil had stopped at a small gas station on the edge of town to fill his truck's tank. As he was walking back from paying, a man he did not know approached him from behind, grabbed his collar, and slammed him against the side of the truck. The man's face was close-close enough that Jamil could smell the sour, acrid scent of old sweat and stale body odour. The man shouted something, but Jamil cannot remember the words. What he remembers are pieces: the rough concrete pressing into his back, the sudden pressure of a hand on his throat, the sound of his own breath going shallow and fast. He remembers his heart hammering so hard in his chest that he thought it might tear through. Then the man shoved him to the ground and walked away. It was over in less than two minutes.

In the weeks that followed, Jamil tried to push the event aside. He told himself it was nothing, that he was fine. He threw himself into the remaining work on the farm-repairing fences, mending equipment, clearing ditches-staying out in the fields from dawn until well after dark. The physical exhaustion helped; when he was too tired to think, the pieces of the memory could not surface. But the moment he stopped, even for a second, his heart would begin to pound again, and the smell of sweat would flood his nose, and he would feel the man's breath on his face. He began to avoid the gas station entirely, driving an extra twenty minutes to a different one on the other side of the county. When November 2nd approached-the anniversary of the assault-he told his wife he had to work and spent the entire day alone in the farthest field, not coming home until he was sure the day had passed.

The worst part, for Jamil, was the way his own body betrayed him. He had always been a steady man, someone who could handle what came. But now, when his heart raced-from climbing a ladder, from lifting a heavy bale, from walking too fast-he would freeze, certain that the attack was about to happen again. He began to watch people more carefully. When a customer at the farmer's market lingered too long near his stall, or when a stranger in town glanced his way, he would scan their hands, their posture, their eyes, looking for the flicker of threat. He started to believe that people could see his fear, that they knew he was weak, and that this made him a target.

At night, alone with his thoughts, he would replay the event again and again, but always in a different way-imagining what he should have done, how he should have fought back, how he could have made the man pay. He would lie awake for hours, his jaw clenched, constructing elaborate scenarios of revenge: tracking the man down, confronting him, making him feel what Jamil had felt. The fantasies gave him a kind of bitter relief, but they also left him hollow and ashamed. He could not explain to his wife why he was so irritable, why he snapped at her for small things, why he would not go to the store with her on weekends. When she asked what was wrong, he would say he was tired, or that the farm was demanding, but the words felt like they came from someone else.

What finally brought Jamil into the clinic was a moment he could no longer dismiss. Two weeks ago, his wife asked him to drive their daughter to the airport. On the highway, a truck backfired, and Jamil's heart began to pound so violently that he had to pull over onto the shoulder. He sat there, gripping the steering wheel, unable to speak, as his daughter asked him if he was okay. He could not tell her what was happening. He could not explain why the sound of that truck had dissolved into a smell of sweat and a feeling of concrete on his back. When he tried to tell his wife later that night, he lost the thread halfway through and fell silent.

He is hoping, now, that talking about it will make the pieces fit together. He is afraid that if he cannot hold the memory in his hands and look at it clearly, it will keep coming for him in fragments, each one a small ambush.
